beats.say: You hear the clatter of horse hooves as Cairo's citadel awakens in 1250, a new Mamluk ruler ascends.
The sultan's secret weapon isn't swords but a network of former slave soldiers turned elite bureaucrats.
In 1260, at the Battle of Ain Jalut, Mamluks use disciplined cavalry to shatter the Mongol advance.
While Europe watches, the Mamluk navy patrols the Red Sea, intercepting Crusader supply ships near Jeddah.
Every year the sultan orders a massive stone inscription, carving his victories into the walls of the Al-Muizz mosque.
1277 sees the Mamluks fund a caravan route across the Sahara, linking Cairo to Timbuktu's gold markets.
The sultan's court rivals any European palace, with jeweled chandeliers casting firelight on Persian carpets.
In 1302, a plague sweeps the city, yet the Mamluks keep tax records immaculate, proving bureaucratic resilience.
The secret to their longevity? Annual military drills on the Nile's floodplain, turning soldiers into river warriors.
When the Ottoman tide rises in 1517, the Mamluk elite dissolve, but their yearly chronicles survive in dusty archives.
